name: Lighthouse of Alexandria (Pharos)
builtBy: Ptolemy I Soter and Ptolemy II Philadelphus
description: A pioneering 100-meter coastal navigational beacon, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
history: Constructed on the limestone island of Pharos at the port of Alexandria, the lighthouse was designed by Greek architect Sostratus of Cnidus. It guided merchant vessels across the Mediterranean for over a millennium using a polished bronze mirror by day and an open fire by night.
construction: Built in three cascading tiers: a square base, an octagonal middle section, and a cylindrical summit topped with a colossal statue of Poseidon or Zeus.
architecture: Constructed from massive blocks of white limestone held together with molten lead mortar, designed to withstand intense sea spray and gale-force Mediterranean storms.
significance: Became the universal archetype for all future lighthouses ('Pharos' remains the root word for lighthouse in French, Spanish, Italian, and Greek).
currentStatus: Severely damaged by earthquakes in 956, 1303, and 1323 CE; stones were salvaged in 1480 CE by Sultan Qaitbay to build the Citadel of Qaitbay.
wonderDesignationYear: c. 225 BCE (Philo of Byzantium & Antipater Lists)
wonderReplacedYear: 1480 CE (Citadel of Qaitbay built on ruins); July 7, 2007 (New 7 Wonders)
wonderReplacedBy: Replaced by modern world registry (New 7 Wonders of the World)
wonderHistoricalContext: Stood proudly as the world's tallest beacon for sixteen centuries until catastrophic earthquakes in 1303 and 1323 CE brought down its lantern. In 1480 CE, Mamluk Sultan Al-Ashraf Qaitbay built a defensive fortress directly over the remaining foundations using the fallen granite blocks.
